column1: 1|CPU compatibility|A replacement processor fits the same general size as the old CPU. What must still be verified before installation?|The motherboard socket, chipset and firmware support the exact CPU|Only that both CPUs use the same brand logo|Only that the CPU cooler has a fan|That the CPU has fewer cores|Physical appearance does not establish compatibility. The socket, board support list and required firmware must support that CPU model.|A socket is the processor's physical and electrical interface; board support also depends on its design and firmware.|A board accepts a CPU only after a supported firmware update. Check the vendor list before purchasing.|Check the exact CPU support list, not just the brand.

1|CPU cache|Which memory is designed to keep frequently used instructions and data close to the CPU for fast access?|CPU cache|A USB flash drive|An optical disc|The RTC battery|Cache reduces the delay of obtaining frequently needed information. It is small, fast memory associated with the processor, not long-term file storage.|Think of cache as a small set of frequently used items kept within immediate reach.|A processor accesses cached data instead of fetching every item from slower main memory.|Cache = small and fast; RAM = larger working memory; storage = persistent files.

1|ECC memory|What is a principal purpose of error-correcting code (ECC) memory in a supported system?|Detect and correct supported memory errors|Convert AC to DC|Make incompatible RAM fit any slot|Store files permanently without power|ECC adds information that enables supported memory-error detection and correction. The platform must support ECC; it is not a substitute for backup.|ECC improves memory reliability by handling certain bit errors.|A supported server platform uses ECC to reduce the effect of correctable memory faults.|ECC concerns memory errors, not permanent file storage.

1|USB-C capabilities|Two laptops have USB-C ports. Why might only one support an external display through that port?|Connector shape does not guarantee the same protocols or capabilities|Every USB-C port has identical video capabilities|The display must use a SATA cable|The laptop with more storage always supports video|USB-C describes the connector. Video output and charging capabilities depend on the implementation and supported modes.|A matching plug shape does not mean every optional function is present.|Check the laptop and dock specifications for supported display output before buying a cable.|Connector type and supported features are separate checks.

1|Expansion slots|Which slot is commonly used for a desktop's discrete graphics card?|A compatible PCI Express x16 slot|A DIMM memory slot|A SATA data port|A CPU socket|A discrete graphics card commonly connects through PCIe. Memory modules and processors use different sockets and cannot substitute for the expansion interface.|PCIe expansion lets compatible devices communicate with the system.|A GPU is fitted into the appropriate PCIe slot, with any required additional power connected.|GPU expansion commonly uses PCIe; RAM goes in DIMM slots.

1|DDR compatibility|Why should a technician not force a DDR4 module into a DDR5 motherboard memory slot?|The generations have different keying and electrical requirements|DDR4 becomes DDR5 when pressed firmly|RAM generations differ only in color|The operating system changes the slot shape|Different DDR generations are not interchangeable merely because both are memory. Mechanical keying helps prevent incompatible installation.|The notch is a compatibility feature, not an obstacle to overcome.|A module's notch does not align. Stop and verify the supported generation.|Never force memory; match the supported DDR generation.

1|Memory channels|A compatible motherboard has four RAM slots. What is the best source for choosing the slots for a two-module dual-channel configuration?|The motherboard manual's recommended population order|Always the two slots closest together|The slots with the darkest plastic on any board|Whichever slots are easiest to reach|Recommended slot placement depends on the board design. The manual identifies the correct pair for the intended configuration.|Memory channels depend on the controller and correct module placement.|The manual recommends A2 and B2; use that pair rather than assuming adjacent slots are correct.|Use the board's population diagram; slot layout is not universal.

1|PSU capacity|When selecting a PSU for a new graphics-card upgrade, what should be considered?|System power needs, suitable connectors and the vendor's requirements|Only the PSU's physical color|Only the monitor's screen size|The number of desktop icons|A PSU must support the full system and provide appropriate connections. A single wattage figure without checking compatibility is insufficient.|The power supply is selected for the system it must power.|A GPU requires dedicated power connectors and higher capacity; check both before upgrading.|Capacity, connectors, quality and compatibility all matter.

1|Mechanical storage|Which part distinguishes a typical mechanical hard drive from an SSD?|Spinning magnetic platters and moving read/write heads|A motherboard CPU socket|A print fuser|A wireless antenna|A mechanical HDD uses moving components to access magnetic storage. SSDs store data electronically without those storage mechanisms.|Mechanical storage moves; solid-state storage does not.|An HDD makes unusual clicking sounds and read errors appear. Protect data and investigate the drive.|HDD = mechanical magnetic storage; SSD = solid-state storage.

1|Firmware storage|Where is motherboard firmware normally stored so it remains available without main power?|Nonvolatile firmware memory on the motherboard|Only in the currently running browser|Only in ordinary volatile RAM|Inside the monitor's display panel|Firmware must remain available when the system is off so it can start the machine. Nonvolatile storage retains its contents without normal system power.|Startup instructions need persistent storage.|A PC can enter firmware setup before any operating system is installed.|Firmware persistence is different from RAM's temporary working data.

2|CPU alignment|What should be done if a CPU does not seat easily in its supported socket?|Check the orientation and alignment marks without forcing it|Push harder until the socket bends|Trim the CPU's edges|Apply power to pull it into place|Correct orientation is essential. Forcing a CPU can damage pins or contacts even when the model is otherwise compatible.|Alignment marks show how a processor must be positioned.|The triangle markers do not align; reposition the CPU before closing the retention mechanism.|Match the orientation and follow the socket instructions.

2|Cooler preparation|A new CPU cooler has a protective film over its contact surface. What must happen before fitting it?|Remove the film according to the cooler instructions|Leave the film as thermal insulation|Add another plastic layer|Connect the film to a SATA port|Protective film is packaging, not a thermal interface. Leaving it in place can obstruct heat transfer.|The cooler needs the intended contact with the CPU through the specified thermal interface.|A new build overheats immediately; inspection finds protective film under the cooler.|Check packaging film, seating and thermal-compound instructions.

2|Rear I/O shield|For a case using a separate snap-in motherboard I/O shield, when is it normally fitted?|Before mounting the motherboard in the case|After all rear cables have been glued in|Inside a memory slot|Over the CPU socket|A separate shield fits the case opening behind the board's ports. Installing it first avoids having to remove the board again; integrated shields differ.|The I/O shield frames the rear connectors; it is not an internal electrical cable.|Check whether the board uses an integrated shield or a separate piece before mounting.|Follow the case/board design; a separate shield normally goes in first.

2|Front-panel wiring|After assembly, the case power button does nothing. The PSU and main power connections check out. What should be checked next?|The power-switch lead on the correct front-panel header pins|The browser's default homepage|The printer paper tray|The monitor's color profile|The case switch signals the motherboard through its front-panel connection. Incorrect placement can prevent the button from triggering startup.|The front-panel switch is a control connection, distinct from the PSU's main power plug.|Use the motherboard pinout to verify the case power-switch connector.|Use the header diagram; do not guess pin positions.

2|Expansion-card power|A newly installed GPU has power sockets specified by its manufacturer. What is the appropriate action?|Connect the required compatible PSU leads before operation|Leave them empty because the monitor provides GPU power|Attach a SATA data cable to them|Force the CPU power plug into any socket|Some GPUs need power in addition to what the slot provides. Use the specified compatible connectors and follow the hardware instructions.|The PCIe slot and supplementary leads may both contribute power.|A GPU displays a missing-power warning; check its specified connections.|Match the device's required power connectors; never force plugs.

2|Loose hardware|A screw falls beneath the motherboard during assembly. What should the technician do before applying power?|Retrieve it and check for other loose conductive parts|Leave it because screws cannot conduct electricity|Shake the powered computer vigorously|Cover the monitor with plastic|A loose metal object can bridge conductors and cause a short. Remove it safely before powering the system.|Conductive debris can turn a physical assembly error into an electrical fault.|Account for dropped screws before closing and powering a case.|No loose conductive hardware inside a powered system.

2|Correct mounting|Why should motherboard screws be tightened only as directed rather than excessively?|Excessive force can damage the board or mounting points|Extra force increases CPU frequency|Screws set the network address|Tighter screws create more RAM capacity|Mounting should secure the board without unnecessary stress. Overtightening can damage components, threads or the circuit board.|Mechanical security does not require excessive force.|Tighten evenly with the correct tool and follow the manufacturer's guidance.|Secure, not forced; avoid stressing the board.

2|Modular PSU cables|A technician replaces one modular PSU with another brand. Which cable practice is safest?|Use cables specifically approved for the new PSU model|Reuse every old modular cable because the plug fits|Choose cables by color alone|Connect any spare cable with force|PSU-side modular pinouts are not universally interchangeable. A fitting connector does not establish electrical compatibility.|The removable cable's PSU end must match that PSU's wiring.|Use the new PSU's supplied or explicitly compatible cables rather than assuming old ones are safe.|Modular PSU cables are not universally interchangeable.

2|CPU-fan header|Where should a standard CPU cooler's fan normally connect when the board manual specifies CPU_FAN?|The motherboard's designated CPU_FAN header|A SATA data port|The clear-CMOS pins|A front-panel audio socket|The designated header powers and monitors the fan according to the board design. Wrong placement can cause monitoring warnings or incorrect control.|Fan headers are functional control and power connections.|The cooler spins but the firmware reports no CPU fan; verify the instructed header and sensor setup.|Use the designated cooler header and the manufacturer's instructions.

2|Final assembly check|Which check is appropriate before a newly assembled PC is powered for the first time?|Verify connections, component seating and clear fan movement|Run a Windows application on the unpowered machine|Place tools on top of the motherboard|Block all vents to reduce dust|A final physical inspection catches preventable wiring, seating and obstruction problems before power is applied.|A short pre-power checklist prevents avoidable faults.|Check RAM latches, power leads, cooler mounting and loose objects before startup.|Inspect before applying power, then test systematically.

3|Boot order|A PC keeps starting the old installed OS instead of the prepared installer USB. What firmware setting is relevant?|Boot-device selection or order|Desktop wallpaper|Printer duplex mode|Mouse pointer speed|Firmware chooses a startup device before the OS runs. Selecting the correct supported media is necessary to launch its installer.|Boot order determines which available startup target is attempted.|Use the one-time boot menu to choose the installer rather than altering unrelated Windows settings.|Boot selection happens before the installed OS loads.

3|Firmware update preparation|Before updating motherboard firmware, which preparation is most important?|Verify the exact model, correct firmware and reliable power|Download firmware for a similar-looking board|Interrupt power repeatedly during the update|Delete customer data to free the CPU cache|Wrong firmware or an interrupted update can leave the system unable to start. Follow the exact vendor procedure and compatibility requirements.|Firmware is foundational startup software, so its update needs careful matching.|Check the board revision and approved update method before flashing.|Exact model, correct update, stable power, vendor procedure.

3|TPM|What is a common role of a Trusted Platform Module (TPM)?|Support secure cryptographic key operations and platform security|Replace the computer's storage drive|Cool the processor|Provide extra Ethernet cable length|A TPM supports security functions involving protected keys and platform integrity. It is not a general-purpose performance upgrade.|Security hardware can help protect key material used by other security features.|A device-encryption deployment checks TPM requirements and recovery-key arrangements.|TPM supports security; it does not replace backups or recovery planning.

3|Hardware virtualization|A compatible hypervisor reports that hardware virtualization is disabled. Where might a technician need to enable it?|The system's UEFI/BIOS virtualization setting|The printer's paper menu|The browser's font settings|A SATA drive's volume label|Supported CPUs may have virtualization features controlled by firmware. Verify platform support and the appropriate setting.|Capability and configuration are separate: a supported feature may still be disabled.|Enable the documented virtualization option, then restart as required and retest.|Check both hardware support and firmware enablement.

3|RAID 5|A healthy RAID 5 array loses one drive. What property can allow it to continue operating in a degraded state?|Distributed parity permits reconstruction of one failed drive's data|Each drive stores an independent full mirror of all files|RAID 5 contains no redundancy|The PSU becomes a replacement storage drive|RAID 5 combines striping with parity and can tolerate one drive failure in the usual configuration. Additional failures during degraded operation can cause loss.|Parity stores information used to reconstruct missing data; it is not a full mirror on every disk.|Replace the failed disk and rebuild according to the controller procedure while maintaining independent backups.|RAID 5: parity, at least three disks, one-disk fault tolerance.

3|RAID 10|What is the usual minimum number of drives for a RAID 10 array combining mirrored pairs with striping?|Four|One|Two|Three|RAID 10 stripes across mirrored pairs. At least two pairs are required, giving the standard four-drive minimum.|It combines mirroring for redundancy with striping across the pairs.|A technician plans two mirrored pairs before creating a striped set across them.|RAID 10 = stripes across mirrors; standard minimum four drives.

3|UPS|Which device can supply temporary battery power during an outage so a PC can shut down gracefully?|Uninterruptible power supply (UPS)|A basic passive power strip|A SATA adapter|A heatsink|A UPS includes stored energy and power-support functions. A simple surge protector does not provide sustained battery power during an outage.|A UPS buys time; it is not an unlimited electricity source.|Configure supported shutdown behavior so work can be saved before the UPS battery is exhausted.|UPS = temporary power during interruption.

3|Surge protection|Why is a surge-protected strip alone insufficient for an extended power outage?|Surge suppression does not supply backup battery energy|It automatically doubles PSU wattage|It stores a full operating-system image|It replaces the laptop charger permanently|Protecting against voltage spikes differs from supplying electricity when mains power disappears.|Different power problems require different protection functions.|Choose suitable backup power when continuity through a short outage is needed.|Surge protection and battery backup are different functions.

3|Firmware password scope|Why should a firmware setup password not be treated as equivalent to full-disk encryption?|Restricting setup access does not itself encrypt stored files|Both always encrypt every file identically|A firmware password increases RAM capacity|Encryption is only a printer feature|An access-control setting and data encryption protect different things. Storage protection requires appropriate encryption and recovery arrangements.|A password prompt is not evidence that the underlying disk contents are encrypted.|A removed unencrypted drive may expose data despite a firmware setup password.|Access restriction is not the same as encryption at rest.

3|Firmware recovery|A firmware change prevents startup. What is the best source for an approved recovery procedure?|The exact motherboard or system manufacturer's documentation|An unrelated printer's user guide|Random pin shorting on a powered board|A guide for any board with the same color|Recovery methods vary by model. Guessing jumper positions or update procedures can make the problem worse.|Hardware recovery needs model-specific instructions.|Consult the documented recovery or reset method and its effect on settings before acting.|Use exact-model recovery guidance, not visual similarity.

4|Controlled troubleshooting|Why is changing one variable at a time useful during diagnosis?|It helps identify which change affects the symptom|It guarantees no backup is needed|It makes all hardware compatible|It avoids the need to test anything|When several things change together, it becomes difficult to identify the cause of an improvement or a new fault.|A controlled test connects evidence to a specific change.|Replace one suspect cable, retest, and record the result before changing a second part.|One controlled change → one interpretable result.

4|Known-good testing|A PC loses network link. Replacing only its cable with a known-good equivalent restores it. What is the best interpretation?|The original cable or its connection is implicated by the test|Every server on the internet has been repaired|The CPU must be replaced immediately|DNS is proven faulty|A known-good substitution isolates a component or connection. It is useful evidence, though final verification and documentation still matter.|Compare a suspect component with an equivalent that works.|Retest with the replacement cable and record stable link operation.|Use equivalent known-good parts to narrow the cause.

4|Intermittent problems|Which information is particularly useful for an intermittent shutdown?|Time, workload, temperatures and relevant logs when it occurs|Only the user's desktop color|The number of files in the recycle bin|The brand of the user's chair|A fault that comes and goes may depend on load, environment or timing. Correlating evidence helps identify the triggering conditions.|Intermittent means conditions matter; capture the pattern.|Shutdowns happen only under heavy load and rising temperatures, directing attention to cooling and power.|Record when, under what conditions, and what changed.

4|Protecting data|Before troubleshooting a failing drive containing important files, what is a priority?|Protect required data using an appropriate approved recovery/backup approach|Run destructive formatting immediately|Defragment repeatedly regardless of symptoms|Delete logs to hide the errors|Troubleshooting can worsen some storage faults. Protecting important data and following an appropriate recovery process comes before avoidable write-intensive or destructive actions.|A repair is not successful if it unnecessarily destroys the customer's data.|Escalate a physically failing drive with critical unbacked data rather than experimenting with destructive tools.|Protect data before risky storage work.

4|Dust removal|What is an appropriate way to choose a computer-cleaning method?|Follow the manufacturer's procedure and ESD precautions|Use water directly on powered circuits|Use any household chemical without checking|Scrape circuit traces with metal tools|Cleaning methods must suit electronics and the device. Inappropriate liquids, tools or static-generating methods can cause damage.|Preventive maintenance must not create a new fault.|Power down as instructed and use approved cleaning tools for vents and components.|Use the device's approved cleaning process.

4|Fan cleaning|When using an approved air-cleaning method on a fan, what precaution may be required?|Keep the fan from overspinning as instructed and avoid damage|Force it to spin as fast as possible|Apply oil to RAM contacts|Use the fan blades as a carrying handle|Uncontrolled airflow can overspin or damage a fan. Follow the manufacturer's guidance for holding or protecting it during cleaning.|Cleaning airflow and normal powered operation are not the same condition.|Clean accumulated dust using the recommended distance and fan-handling precautions.|Clean fans safely; do not use compressed air to race them.

4|No-power diagnosis|A desktop is completely unresponsive. Which is an appropriate initial check?|Verify the outlet, power cable and PSU switch|Reinstall the browser first|Replace the CPU before checking power|Format the SSD|A system cannot start without incoming power. Checking the external supply path is a simple relevant first step.|Start with basic prerequisites before costly replacements.|A switched-off PSU rocker explains a no-power condition without an internal component failure.|No power: verify the external power path first.

4|After-service fault|A PC starts overheating immediately after its cooler was removed and refitted. What should be checked first?|Cooler seating, fan connection and thermal interface|The printer's queue length|The DNS search suffix|The monitor's wallpaper|The recent change is strong diagnostic evidence. An improperly mounted cooler or fan connection can explain the new temperature fault.|Ask what changed just before the symptom started.|Inspection finds the fan lead disconnected after cooler servicing.|Correlate the fault with the most recent relevant change.

4|Memory testing|Random crashes suggest a possible RAM fault. Which next step provides relevant evidence?|Run an appropriate supported memory diagnostic|Change the keyboard language|Replace the monitor cable automatically|Disable all backups permanently|A memory diagnostic can help test the suspected subsystem. Crashes alone are not proof of defective RAM.|Symptoms suggest a theory; testing supplies evidence.|Use a supported memory test and assess results alongside seating and compatibility checks.|Suspected RAM faults should be tested, not assumed.

4|Stop-work condition|A technician notices a burning smell and visible damage while a computer is operating. What is the appropriate response?|Stop use, isolate power safely and follow the incident/service procedure|Continue stress testing to make the smell stronger|Cover the vents with paper|Open the PSU while it remains connected|Continuing operation may worsen an electrical fault. Safe isolation and qualified assessment take priority over routine diagnosis.|Some symptoms require stopping work rather than continuing ordinary tests.|Power is safely isolated and the damaged unit is routed for approved assessment.|Smoke, burning or electrical damage: stop and follow safe procedures.

5|TCP|Which transport protocol provides an ordered, reliable byte stream between applications?|TCP|UDP|ARP|DHCP|TCP uses mechanisms including sequencing and retransmission to provide reliable ordered delivery. UDP does not provide the same transport guarantees.|Transport protocols provide different communication services.|A file-transfer application needs delivered data in order and uses TCP.|TCP = reliable ordered stream; UDP = datagrams without those guarantees.

5|UDP|Which statement describes UDP at the transport layer?|It sends datagrams without TCP-style connection setup and delivery guarantees|It guarantees retransmission of every lost datagram|It always encrypts every message|It assigns motherboard addresses|UDP provides datagram transport without built-in ordered reliable delivery. Applications can implement extra behavior themselves.|A lightweight transport can favor timely sending over waiting for retransmissions.|A real-time application may tolerate some loss rather than delaying every update.|UDP itself does not guarantee delivery or order.

5|HTTPS port|Which TCP port is conventionally associated with HTTPS?|443|22|25|110|HTTPS conventionally uses TCP 443 for secure web communication. Other listed ports serve different common purposes.|A port identifies a service endpoint, not a physical connector.|A firewall rule for a conventional HTTPS service allows its required TCP destination port.|HTTPS commonly uses TCP 443.

5|SSH port|Which service conventionally uses TCP port 22 for secure remote administration?|SSH|Plain HTTP|DNS zone transfer by default|POP3|SSH commonly uses TCP 22 and provides encrypted remote access. A port number alone still does not prove a service's identity.|Remote-management protocols differ in purpose and protection.|An administrator selects SSH rather than an unencrypted remote terminal protocol.|SSH commonly uses TCP 22.

5|DNS transport|Which port is conventionally used by DNS over UDP or TCP?|53|80|3389|445|Traditional DNS uses port 53 and can use UDP or TCP. Treating DNS as UDP-only overlooks supported TCP uses.|One service can use more than one transport.|A network must permit the DNS traffic required by its design rather than assuming every lookup uses only one transport.|Traditional DNS: port 53, UDP and TCP.

5|DHCP ports|Which UDP port pair is associated with DHCPv4 servers and clients?|Server 67 and client 68|Server 443 and client 22|Server 25 and client 110|Server 3389 and client 445|DHCPv4 uses UDP 67 on the server side and 68 on the client side. These support configuration exchange, not name resolution.|DHCP has distinct client and server communication roles.|An address-allocation capture shows DHCP messages between the client and server port pair.|DHCPv4 = UDP 67/68.

5|Switch forwarding|What information does a typical Ethernet switch use to learn which port leads to a local device?|Source MAC addresses observed in frames|The user's password|The file extension of attachments|The monitor resolution|A switch learns source MAC addresses on ingress ports and uses its forwarding information for destination frames.|MAC addresses support local Ethernet delivery.|After a PC sends a frame, the switch can associate its source MAC with the receiving port.|Switch learning uses source MAC addresses and ingress ports.

5|Wireless access point|What is a typical role of a wireless access point?|Connect wireless clients to a network|Convert all DC electricity to AC|Replace the CPU's arithmetic unit|Provide toner to printers|An AP provides wireless network access and typically bridges clients into the associated network. Routing and internet service may be separate functions.|Wireless access and routing are distinct roles even when one home device combines them.|An office adds APs for Wi-Fi coverage while retaining its existing router.|AP = wireless access; router = forwards between networks.

5|Fiber and interference|Why might fiber be selected for a link near strong electromagnetic interference?|It carries optical signals and is not subject to EMI pickup like copper conductors|It never needs compatible transceivers|It powers all connected devices automatically|It has no installation limits|Fiber transmits light rather than electrical data signals in copper. Compatible optics, distance and installation requirements still apply.|Choose a medium for the environment, not only the connector's appearance.|A link near industrial equipment uses suitable fiber and optics.|Fiber resists electromagnetic interference but still needs compatible equipment.

5|Subnet capacity|How many conventional usable host addresses are in an IPv4 /26 subnet?|62|64|126|254|A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 gives 64 addresses. For a conventional subnet, subtract the network and broadcast addresses to get 62 usable hosts.|Prefix length determines how many bits remain for hosts.|A segment requiring 50 host addresses fits within a conventional /26 capacity.|For /26: 32−26=6; 2^6−2=62.

6|Local versus remote|A host is 192.168.10.20/24. Which destination is in its local subnet?|192.168.10.200|192.168.11.20|192.168.20.10|10.0.0.20|With /24, the first three octets identify this network. 192.168.10.200 shares that network portion.|Use the mask rather than guessing from one matching number.|The host can attempt local delivery to 192.168.10.200 without treating it as a remote subnet.|For this /24, local addresses share 192.168.10.

6|Prefix conversion|Which dotted-decimal subnet mask corresponds to /26?|255.255.255.192|255.255.255.0|255.255.0.0|255.255.255.252|A /26 has 24 one-bits in the first three octets and two more in the last. Binary 11000000 is decimal 192.|A prefix is the count of leading network bits.|Convert /26 by writing 26 leading ones rather than memorizing an unrelated host count.|/26 = 255.255.255.192.

6|Broadcast address|What is the broadcast address for 192.168.10.0/24?|192.168.10.255|192.168.10.0|192.168.10.1|192.168.11.255|In this /24, all host bits set to one produce .255. The .0 address is the network address.|Broadcast and network addresses occupy distinct roles in a conventional subnet.|Do not assign 192.168.10.255 as an ordinary host on that /24.|For 192.168.10.0/24: network .0; broadcast .255.

6|DNS testing|Which Windows command is intended to query DNS records during troubleshooting?|nslookup|format|taskkill|diskpart clean|nslookup queries DNS, providing relevant evidence for name-resolution problems. The other commands act on processes or storage.|Test the service that matches the symptom.|An IP works but a name fails; query that name with nslookup and inspect the response.|nslookup = DNS query tool.

6|Route tracing|Which Windows command helps identify the sequence of router hops toward a destination?|tracert|sfc /scannow|mkdir|chkdsk|tracert probes the path and reports responding hops. Missing replies may reflect filtering, so output needs interpretation.|A path test differs from checking only one endpoint.|A technician compares where responses stop along a route, while considering ICMP filtering.|tracert explores the path; ping tests echo reachability.

6|IPv4 loopback|Which address is commonly used to test the local IPv4 loopback interface?|127.0.0.1|169.254.0.0|255.255.255.255|192.0.2.255|127.0.0.1 refers to the local host through loopback. A successful loopback test does not prove the physical network works.|A local networking-stack test can succeed with the cable unplugged.|Ping loopback while diagnosing local networking, then test the actual interface and network separately.|Loopback success is not proof of external connectivity.

6|DHCP renewal|Which command requests renewal of a Windows DHCP configuration on applicable adapters?|ipconfig /renew|ipconfig /flushdns|sfc /scannow|tasklist|/renew requests DHCP renewal; /flushdns clears cached DNS resolver entries. They address different functions.|An address lease and a cached name lookup are different things.|After fixing a DHCP connectivity issue, request renewal and inspect the resulting configuration.|/renew = DHCP lease; /flushdns = resolver cache.

6|Isolating name-resolution faults|A client reaches an external service by IP but cannot resolve its hostname. What should be investigated next?|DNS configuration and name-resolution responses|The CPU cooler's paint color|Printer paper alignment|The mouse battery only|Successful IP communication narrows the issue, while failed lookup specifically points toward DNS investigation. It does not prove every network component is healthy.|Separate addressing/connectivity tests from name-resolution tests.|Use ipconfig /all and nslookup to inspect the configured DNS path.|IP works, name fails: investigate DNS.

6|NAT|What does IPv4 NAT commonly do on an internet gateway?|Translate addresses between an internal network and another addressing domain|Turn every Ethernet frame into an optical pulse|Replace all authentication controls|Assign the CPU's clock frequency|NAT changes address information according to a translation policy. It is not itself a replacement for a complete firewall or authentication design.|Private addressing and public-facing communication can use translation.|Several internal clients access services through a gateway's translation rules.|NAT translates addresses; it does not mean all traffic is safe.

6|SSID|What does a Wi-Fi SSID primarily identify?|The wireless network's name|A guarantee that the network is encrypted|The client's CPU serial number|The DNS server's password|An SSID labels a wireless network. The name alone does not authenticate the operator or establish encryption strength.|A familiar label can be copied by another transmitter.|Verify the intended network and its security rather than trusting a name alone.|SSID = network name, not proof of trust.

7|Airplane mode|A laptop's Wi-Fi suddenly stops after a key combination is pressed. What is a useful initial check?|Airplane mode and wireless enable settings|Whether the printer has toner|The SSD's file-system label|The CPU socket type|A wireless-disable control can stop connectivity without a failed adapter. Check settings and recent actions first.|A configuration switch can look like hardware failure.|Re-enable wireless if it was unintentionally disabled, then reconnect and test.|Check wireless controls before replacing the adapter.

7|Brightness control|A laptop display is dim after a function-key press, but an image is clearly present. What should be checked first?|Brightness settings and the relevant function-key controls|Repartition the drive immediately|Replace the router|Format a USB drive|The timing and symptom suggest a setting change before a component replacement. Check the simple control first.|Recent changes provide diagnostic clues.|Restore brightness using the documented keys or display settings and retest.|A dim screen may be a setting, not a failed display.

7|Battery disposal|How should a removed laptop battery be disposed of?|Through an approved battery recycling or disposal process|In an ordinary fire|By puncturing it to release stored charge|In water with household waste|Batteries require appropriate handling and disposal. Burning or puncturing them can create hazards.|Disposal is part of safe servicing, not an afterthought.|Use the organization's or manufacturer's approved collection route.|Use approved battery disposal; do not puncture or burn.

7|Hibernate versus sleep|Which statement normally describes hibernation?|It saves session state to storage for later resume with power removed|It keeps all session data only in powered RAM|It permanently deletes all open documents|It installs a new OS|Hibernation stores the session state on persistent storage. Sleep typically retains the session in powered memory, with platform-specific behavior.|Different low-power states preserve work differently.|A user chooses supported hibernation before an extended period without external power.|Hibernate saves state to storage; sleep normally relies on retained memory power.

7|Storage upgrade preparation|Before replacing a laptop's system drive, what should be planned?|Data backup, recovery/installation media and hardware compatibility|Only the desktop background|A printer toner refill|An unrelated Wi-Fi password reset|Replacing the system drive affects data and startup. Compatible hardware and a recovery path must be prepared.|An upgrade includes migration and recovery, not just swapping hardware.|Verify required files and installation/recovery tools before removing the old drive.|Protect data and plan how the new drive will boot.

7|Laptop antenna leads|While replacing an internal Wi-Fi card, what should guide antenna-lead handling?|The exact service manual's connector positions and removal method|Pulling on the wires as hard as possible|Connecting antenna leads to RAM contacts|Choosing any screw as the antenna socket|Small antenna connectors and leads are easily damaged. Follow the model-specific procedure and documented placement.|Serviceable parts can still have fragile connections.|Record lead positions and disconnect using the approved technique.|Follow the manual; do not pull fragile connectors by their wires.

7|Touchpad controls|A laptop touchpad stops responding while an external mouse works. What is an appropriate initial check?|Touchpad enable settings and any hardware/function-key toggle|Replace the CPU immediately|Erase the drive|Open the PSU|A disabled touchpad can explain the symptom without a hardware failure.
